definition: A simple reference model or policy a measured result must beat; without one, an impressive score may just restate how easy the problem is.
example: Predicting next week equals this week is the seasonal-naive baseline for the demand forecaster.

definition: Data deliberately excluded from training and tuning, scored once at the end to estimate performance on cases nobody has seen yet.
example: The churn model's final cost curve comes from a 20% holdout untouched during feature selection.

definition: Replaying history in time order to score a strategy using only information available at each simulated decision point.
example: The demand model trains through October, scores November, then re-trains through November before scoring December.

definition: A range around an estimate that quantifies sampling uncertainty; a 95% interval contains the true value about 19 times in 20.
example: The 4.23% mean gap carries a 95% CI of 3.1–5.3 percentage points across the 56 instances.

definition: Weighted absolute percentage error: total absolute forecast error divided by total actual volume, so busy series outweigh sparse ones.
example: A WAPE of 0.157 means the forecast misses by 15.7% of total demand across every store combined.

definition: Mean absolute scaled error: model error divided by the error of a naive seasonal forecast, so 1.0 means no improvement over naive.
example: MASE 0.84 means the model's error is 84% of what the seasonal-naive forecast achieves.

definition: The unweighted mean of per-class F1 scores, giving rare classes the same vote as frequent ones when averaging performance.
example: The news tagger reports 0.946 macro-F1 so a rare topic counts as much as a common one.

definition: The share of relevant items that appear within the top five candidates a system retrieves or recommends.
example: Recall@5 of 0.83 means 83% of the evidence a human would cite appears in the agent's top five retrievals.

definition: The causal effect of an action on one person: the difference between what they do with it and what they would have done without.
example: A customer who renews with the email might have renewed anyway; only the difference is uplift.

definition: Cumulative true uplift captured when people are contacted in predicted-uplift order; its lift over the random line shows targeting value.
example: Mailing the top 30% by Qini ranking captures most of the campaign's measured profit advantage.

definition: The percentage a solution's cost sits above the best-known or proven-optimal cost for that same problem instance.
example: A routing plan 4.23% above best-known distance has a 4.23% optimality gap.

definition: The 50th and 95th percentile response times: half of requests answer faster than p50, and 19 of 20 faster than p95.
example: p95 of 380 ms means one request in twenty is slower than 380 ms even on a healthy server.

definition: How closely predicted probabilities match observed frequencies; among events scored 0.3, roughly 30% should actually happen.
example: If 100 customers scored near 0.3 churn risk and about 30 churn, the risk scores are calibrated.

definition: A baseline forecast that repeats the last observed seasonal cycle, so tomorrow equals the same weekday last week; the minimum bar a model must beat.
example: The demand study requires beating next-week-equals-this-week before any model ships.

definition: A prediction interval built from held-out residuals, guaranteed to cover roughly the stated share of future points without assuming any error distribution.
example: The workbench's 80% band around the LightGBM curve comes from held-out calibration residuals.

definition: A method that adjusts forecasts at every hierarchy level so they add up consistently, weighting corrections by the covariance of historical errors.
example: Store, region, and total forecasts are MinT-adjusted so every level reports the same demand.

definition: Adaptive large neighborhood search: a metaheuristic that repeatedly destroys part of a solution and repairs it, adapting which neighborhoods pay off.
example: The routing solver removes 20–40% of the stops per iteration and keeps the repair only if distance improves.

definition: Vehicle routing problem with time windows: serve every customer within an allowed time slot while minimizing distance or fleet size.
example: The Solomon benchmarks give each customer a time window; C101 is the tightest instance.

definition: Expected calibration error: the average gap between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies across probability bins; lower means better-calibrated scores.
example: After Platt scaling, customers scored 0.3 churn near 0.3 actually churn — the ECE drops.

definition: An uplift model that trains one model per arm, treated and control, and scores each person as the difference between the two predictions.
example: The Hillstrom study trains one spend model on the emailed group and one on the control group, then subtracts.

definition: Controlled-experiment using pre-experiment data: a variance-reduction technique that adjusts each subject's outcome by a coefficient times a pre-period covariate.
example: Adjusting on pre-campaign spend shrinks the Hillstrom experiment's confidence interval by about half.

definition: Reducing model weights to lower-precision numbers, such as 4-bit, so inference uses less memory and bandwidth, trading a small quality loss for speed.
example: Q4_K_M quantisation cuts the served model's memory footprint to roughly a quarter of fp16.

definition: A monitoring view that tracks a model's inputs, predictions, and quality metrics over time, flagging when live data departs from the training distribution.
example: The anomaly demo plots input drift so threshold decay is visible instead of assumed.

definition: An F1 variant for range-based anomaly detection that credits detectors for finding whole event windows, not just isolated anomalous points.
example: Flagging any point inside a labeled taxi-outage window earns the detector partial range-F1 credit.

definition: An agent pattern that alternates planning the next step, acting with tools, and reviewing the result before deciding what to do next.
example: The workflow agent plans a search, calls the tool, checks the citation, then continues or backtracks.
